title: Crafting Offers - Connecting Needs with Funding
subtitle: Being an Honest Broker
description: Master the art of identifying implementer needs, understanding funder priorities, and crafting compelling proposals that connect problems with resources.
learningObjectives: Map the DPI funding ecosystem and understand different funder motivations
Identify real needs beyond stated wants using probing questions
Find genuine sweet spots where implementer needs meet funder priorities
Design compelling offers with clear problems, theories of change, and realistic plans
Write proposals that funders actually read and approve
Manage risks and address objections constructively
Ensure funded proposals transition to successful implementation

content.overview: Success in DPI work often depends on connecting implementers with funders. This requires deep understanding of the funding landscape - who funds what, why, and how. Different funders have fundamentally different motivations, constraints, and decision criteria. A proposal that excites Gates Foundation may bore World Bank. Understanding this landscape is the foundation of offer crafting.

keyPoints.title: Multilateral Development Banks (World Bank, ADB, AfDB, IDB)
keyPoints.description: Large-scale loans focused on economic development and institutional capacity building
characteristics: Motivation: Economic development, poverty reduction, institutional strengthening
Funding type: Primarily loans (with grant components for poorest countries)
Typical size: $10M - $500M
Timeline: 12-24 months from concept to approval
Decision drivers: Country creditworthiness, government ownership, economic impact, fiduciary safeguards
Constraints: Government debt capacity, procurement rules, safeguard policies
keyPoints.sweetSpot: This helps government deliver better services while building institutional capacity
examples: World Bank funds $50M digital government transformation in Rwanda with focus on institutional capacity building and economic impact measurement
Asian Development Bank provides $30M loan for Philippines national ID system with emphasis on financial inclusion outcomes

keyPoints.title: Bilateral Development Agencies (USAID, DFID/FCDO, GIZ, AFD)
keyPoints.description: Grants and technical assistance aligned with donor country foreign policy objectives
characteristics: Motivation: Foreign policy objectives, development goals, commercial interests
Funding type: Grants, technical assistance
Typical size: $500K - $50M
Timeline: 6-18 months from concept to approval
Decision drivers: Alignment with donor priorities, geopolitical considerations, demonstration value
Constraints: Must align with bilateral relationship and donor country priorities
keyPoints.sweetSpot: This advances both development outcomes and [donor country] foreign policy goals
examples: USAID funds $15M digital health program in Kenya that strengthens US-Kenya partnership on health security
FCDO supports $8M digital land registry in Tanzania with focus on women's land rights and UK development priorities

keyPoints.title: Philanthropic Foundations (Gates, Omidyar, Rockefeller)
keyPoints.description: Mission-driven grants focused on innovation and scalable solutions
characteristics: Motivation: Specific mission focus (Gates: health, agriculture; Omidyar: governance, digital economy)
Funding type: Grants
Typical size: $100K - $20M
Timeline: 3-12 months from concept to approval
Decision drivers: Theory of change alignment, scalability potential, innovation, leadership quality
Constraints: Must fit foundation's specific theory of change
keyPoints.sweetSpot: This pilot innovation could transform [foundation focus area] at scale globally
examples: Gates Foundation funds $12M for India's Aadhaar-based vaccine delivery system with potential for global replication
Omidyar Network provides $5M for open-source digital identity platform (MOSIP) that can be adopted by multiple countries

keyPoints.title: UN Agencies (UNDP, UNICEF, WHO, ITU)
keyPoints.description: Technical assistance and coordination focused on mandate-specific development goals
characteristics: Motivation: Mandate-specific development goals (health, children, telecom)
Funding type: Technical assistance, small grants, convening
Typical size: $50K - $5M
Timeline: 3-9 months
Decision drivers: Alignment with agency mandate, government request, regional/global benefit
Constraints: Must fit agency mandate, often requires government co-funding
keyPoints.sweetSpot: This helps government meet [SDG/international standard] with our technical guidance
examples: UNICEF supports $2M child-focused digital services in Bangladesh aligned with SDG targets for children
UNDP provides $3M technical assistance for digital governance capacity building in Pacific islands

keyPoints.title: Impact Investors and Blended Finance (IFC, CDC, DFC, Convergence)
keyPoints.description: Equity, debt, and guarantees for revenue-generating DPI with development impact
characteristics: Motivation: Financial return + development impact
Funding type: Equity, debt, guarantees
Typical size: $1M - $100M
Timeline: 6-18 months
Decision drivers: Path to financial sustainability, market viability demonstration, development impact
Constraints: Must have credible path to returns
keyPoints.sweetSpot: This creates sustainable market for DPI while delivering public benefit
examples: IFC invests $25M equity in payment infrastructure company serving underbanked populations
CDC provides $10M debt financing for digital credit platform with demonstrated social impact

grantsVsLoans.grants: Free money, but often smaller, shorter-term, focused on innovation and pilots
grantsVsLoans.loans: Larger scale, longer-term, but add to government debt and require repayment
grantsVsLoans.guidance: Pilots and innovations → grants; Infrastructure and scale → loans

technicalAssistance.description: Funding for advisors, consultants, capacity building (not infrastructure)
technicalAssistance.example: World Bank loan + embedded technical advisors

blendedFinance.description: Combining grants (catalytic, high-risk) with loans/equity (larger-scale, lower-risk)
blendedFinance.example: Gates grant for pilot + World Bank loan for scale

content.keyInsight: Different funders have different motivations, constraints, and decision criteria. Understanding this landscape is essential - you need to match the right funder to the right need, not force-fit a square peg into a round hole.

exercises.prompt: Choose a DPI project you're familiar with. Map which funders might be appropriate and why. For each funder, identify: (1) What about this project aligns with their priorities? (2) What constraints might they have? (3) How would you frame the project for them specifically?

Find a real DPI project that received funding. Research: Who funded it and why? What was the funder's motivation? How was it framed in the proposal? Could it have been funded differently with a different funder?

modules.title: Need Identification - Beyond What They Say They Want

content.overview: Governments often ask for specific solutions: 'We need blockchain' or 'We need what India built.' But these are wants, not needs. Your job is to understand the underlying need - the actual problem to solve. Funders fund needs (problems), not wants (specific solutions). Understanding true needs allows you to craft better, more fundable offers.

keyPoints.title: The Problem: Stated Wants ≠ Actual Needs
keyPoints.description: Government says 'We need a new digital identity system' but what they might actually need is better integration of existing systems, cleaner data, or improved service delivery that happens to require identity.
whyItMatters: Funders fund needs (problems to solve), not wants (specific solutions)
Proposing stated wants without understanding needs may solve the wrong problem
Understanding true needs allows better, more fundable offers

probingQuestions: What problem are you really trying to solve?
examples.actualNeed: Reducing fraud and building trust in land records (technology-agnostic)
examples.insight: Need is fraud reduction and trust, not specifically blockchain - opens up more solution options

examples.statedWant: We need foreign consultants to design our health information system
probingQuestions: What have you tried with local capacity?
examples.actualNeed: Specific technical expertise in distributed systems architecture, not general consulting
examples.insight: Targeted technical assistance is more fundable than vague 'foreign consultants'

categories.name: The Why Chain
questions: Why do you need [X]?
What problem does that solve?
Why is that problem important?
What happens if you don't solve it?
categories.purpose: Drill down from solution to root cause

categories.name: Current State Constraints
questions: What have you tried already?
What's preventing you from solving this now?
What resources do you currently have?
What would you do if you had unlimited budget?

categories.name: Success Criteria
questions: How will you know this succeeded?
What would change if this works?
Who benefits and how?
What's the measurable impact?
categories.purpose: Define concrete outcomes, not vague aspirations

example.question: What would successful digital transformation look like in 3 years?
example.response: Citizens can access 20 government services online, wait times reduced by 70%, corruption complaints down 50%
example.insight: Need is specific service improvements with measurable outcomes - far more compelling than vague 'digital transformation'

patterns.description: They ask for technology, but underlying need is capacity to use it
patterns.example: Request: 'We need data analytics platform' → Actual need: platform + training + change management + sustained technical support

patterns.description: They ask for 2-year project, but need permanent capability
patterns.example: Request: 'We need advisors for 2 years' → Actual need: advisory support + knowledge transfer + local capacity building for long-term sustainability

patterns.description: They ask for technical solution, but need political coalition
patterns.example: Request: 'We need interoperability standards' → Actual need: standards + coalition of ministries who'll adopt them + governance structure

patterns.description: They ask for standalone solution, but need integration with existing systems
patterns.example: Request: 'We need payment gateway' → Actual need: gateway + integration with 5 existing government systems + migration plan

keyPoints.title: Validating Needs Through Multiple Perspectives
keyPoints.guidance: Don't trust single source. Talk to actual users, technical implementers, and oversight bodies.

example.scenario: Ministry of Education wants tablets for every student

perspectives.view: We need tablets for every student
We need reliable electricity and internet first, then we can use tablets
We don't have capacity to manage 500,000 tablets
We don't have budget for ongoing tablet replacement every 3 years

example.realNeed: Not tablets, but improving learning outcomes - achievable through teacher training, better curriculum, or different technology approach

keyPoints.title: Red Flags: When 'Needs' Are Solutions in Disguise

flags.redFlag: Copying someone else - 'We need what India built' or 'We need what Estonia has'
flags.realNeed: Solve similar problem, but context differs - need adapted solution
Capability that vendor provides (but other solutions might work too)

flags.redFlag: Budget-driven - 'We have $5M to spend on digital transformation'
flags.realNeed: Specific outcomes (budget is input, not need)

keyPoints.title: From Needs to Fundable Problem Statements

characteristics: Specific and measurable
Clearly articulated beneficiaries
Outcomes-focused (not technology-focused)
Aligned with funder priorities
Evidence-based (data showing scale of problem)

transformations.strong: 5 million citizens can't access government services because they lack documentation. This prevents healthcare access, education enrollment, and financial inclusion. We need to establish reliable digital identity that enables service access while protecting privacy.

Citizens wait average 6 hours at government offices for services that should take 20 minutes. This costs economy $200M/year in lost productivity. We need to digitize high-volume services to reduce wait times by 80% and improve citizen satisfaction.

Our government systems crash during peak periods (tax filing deadline, exam results), causing citizen frustration and revenue loss. We need scalable, reliable infrastructure to ensure services are available when citizens need them.

content.keyInsight: Funders fund needs (problems), not wants (solutions). Your job is to understand the real need, articulate it compellingly, and then design an offer that addresses it. This requires asking hard questions, validating across stakeholders, and resisting the urge to jump to solutions prematurely.

exercises.prompt: Partner exercise: One person plays a government official requesting 'blockchain for our supply chain.' Other person plays offer crafter using probing questions to reveal the actual need. After 10 minutes, switch roles with a different scenario.

Take a real project proposal you've seen. Identify: (1) What solution did they request? (2) What probing questions would you ask? (3) What might the underlying need actually be? (4) How would you reframe the problem statement to be more fundable?

modules.title: The Sweet Spot - Where Implementer Needs Meet Funder Priorities

content.overview: Once you understand both implementer needs and funder priorities, your job is to find the overlap - the sweet spot where you can honestly say: 'This offer meets your actual need AND aligns with funder's priorities.' If you can't say that honestly, keep looking for different framing or different funder.

keyPoints.title: Finding the Overlap: The Sweet Spot Framework
keyPoints.description: Same underlying need can be framed differently for different funders

example.implementerNeed: Ministry of Health needs health information system to track patient care, reduce duplicate data entry, improve diagnosis, and enable telemedicine in rural areas

funderOptions.sweetSpot: Health information system strengthens institutional capacity to deliver healthcare efficiently while improving population health outcomes

funderOptions.priorities: Global health data, disease surveillance, innovations in health delivery
funderOptions.sweetSpot: Health information system enables real-time disease surveillance and telemedicine innovations that can be replicated globally

funderOptions.priorities: Health outcomes in partner countries, COVID response capacity
funderOptions.sweetSpot: Health information system improves health outcomes in [country] while strengthening resilience to future pandemics

example.insight: Same need, different framing for different funders - all honest and accurate

funders.name: World Bank
criteria: Fiduciary soundness (can government manage funds properly?)
framingGuidance: Lead with government ownership: 'Government of [X] requests...'
Emphasize institutional capacity: 'This builds permanent capability within Ministry...'
Show economic impact: 'Improving service delivery will increase productivity by...'
Demonstrate fiduciary readiness: 'Established procurement unit with track record...'

funders.name: Gates Foundation
criteria: Theory of change (clear logic from activity → outcome → impact)
framingGuidance: Start with problem and theory of change: '70% of citizens lack healthcare access. Digital health records enable...'
Highlight innovation: 'First application of offline-capable health records in low-connectivity contexts...'
Show global potential: 'If successful, this approach could be replicated in 20 similar countries...'
Feature strong leadership: 'Led by Dr. [X], recognized expert in...'

funders.name: USAID
framingGuidance: Connect to bilateral relationship: 'Strengthens [country]-U.S. partnership on digital development...'
Emphasize sustainability: 'Builds local capacity to sustain after USAID support ends...'
Show measurable outcomes: 'Will improve healthcare access for 2 million citizens in 3 years...'
Highlight demonstration value: 'Proof of concept for digital health across region...'

keyPoints.title: When There's No Sweet Spot

scenarios.situation: Implementer needs funding now, funder's funding cycle opens in 9 months
scenarios.action: Look for bridge funding or different funder

scenarios.situation: Implementer needs $50M, funder maximum grant is $5M
scenarios.action: Break into phases, or find co-funders

scenarios.situation: Implementer wants government-operated system, funder prioritizes private sector and markets
scenarios.action: Find different funder or redesign approach

scenarios.situation: Implementer in Country X, funder only funds in Countries Y and Z

keyPoints.keyDecision: If you can't find genuine sweet spot, don't force it. Crafting offer that doesn't meet implementer need is dishonest. Crafting offer that doesn't fit funder priority wastes everyone's time. It's okay to say 'I don't think there's a fit here.'

keyPoints.title: Multi-Stakeholder Sweet Spots
keyPoints.complexity: More than two parties - multiple implementers and funders

example.scenario: Digital ID System with multiple parties

stakeholders.need: Needs digital ID for government services
Needs contract and validation for their technology

stakeholders.priority: Wants innovation and global public good

multiPartySweetSpot: Government gets digital ID system (meets their need)
Bhashini gets contract to provide technology (meets their need)
World Bank funds government capacity building (meets their priority)
Gates funds technology innovation component (meets their priority)
USAID funds bilateral technical assistance (meets their priority)
example.challenge: More parties = more complexity to manage, but also more resources available

keyPoints.title: Integrity Check: Are You Being an Honest Broker?

characteristics: Finds genuine alignment between implementer needs and funder priorities
Transparent about trade-offs and constraints
Serves both parties equally
Creates win-win outcomes
honestBroker.test: If both parties fully understood each other, would they still agree? If yes → honest broker. If no → you're hiding something from someone.

toAvoid: Telling implementer what funder wants to hear, regardless of reality
Promising funder outcomes that implementer can't deliver
Changing implementer's real needs to match funder priorities
Hiding risks or challenges from either party

content.keyInsight: The sweet spot is where you can honestly say: 'This offer meets your actual need AND aligns with funder's priorities.' If you can't say that honestly, keep looking for different framing or different funder. Being an honest broker means serving both parties with integrity.

exercises.prompt: Choose a real DPI need from a country you know. Map 3 different funders who might support it. For each funder: (1) What are their priorities? (2) How would you frame this need for them specifically? (3) What would be the sweet spot framing? Be specific and honest.

Think of a case where you've seen someone force-fit a proposal to a funder (or been tempted to do so yourself). What was the mismatch? What would honesty have required? What was the consequence of the force-fit?

content.overview: Once you've identified needs and found the sweet spot with a funder, you need to design the actual offer - structuring it with clear problem, approach, outcomes, and value proposition. A strong offer design is both ambitious (worth doing) and achievable (can actually be done).

keyPoints.title: Component 1: Problem Statement
elements: What's the current impact (cost, harm, inefficiency)?
Why hasn't it been solved yet?
Why is now the right time?

example.strong: Uganda's tax collection rate is 42% of potential revenue - $1.2B annually uncollected. The challenge is not policy but implementation: 67% of businesses operate informally, invisible to tax authority. Current manual registration requires 14 days and 12 documents, deterring compliance. Digital business registration could reduce registration time to 2 hours and documents to 3, bringing 200,000 informal businesses into tax system over 3 years, increasing revenue by $380M annually.
whyStrong: Root cause identified (registration friction, not policy)

keyPoints.title: Component 2: Theory of Change
keyPoints.framework: IF we do X (intervention) THEN Y will happen (immediate outcome) WHICH WILL lead to Z (ultimate impact) BECAUSE of this logic (assumptions and evidence)

example.intervention: IF we implement digital business registration (2 hours, 3 documents)
example.outcome: THEN informal businesses will register formally (reducing registration friction from 14 days to 2 hours)
example.impact: WHICH WILL increase tax revenue by $380M over 3 years (200K new taxpayers × $1,900 avg annual tax)
example.logic: BECAUSE research shows registration friction is primary barrier to formalization (World Bank Doing Business data) and formalized businesses pay taxes (Uganda Revenue Authority data)
assumptionsToValidate: Businesses want to formalize if friction is low
Businesses will pay taxes once registered
Tax authority can handle 200K new taxpayers
Digital registration is reliable and accessible

included: Training for tax officials and business support organizations
M&E system to track registrations and tax revenue
notIncluded: Addressing corruption in tax administration (related but different)
structure.whyScopeBoundariesMatter: Prevents mission creep and clarifies what you're responsible for vs what's outside your control

outcomes: Digital registration platform operational in 5 major cities
Registration time reduced from 14 days to <4 hours
70% of new registrations via digital channel

impacts: Model for digital government services across sectors

outcomeDefinitions.outcome: What changes for beneficiaries (time saved, formalization)
outcomeDefinitions.impact: Broader societal change (revenue increase, business environment)

keyPoints.title: Component 5: Value Proposition
forGovernment: $380M annual revenue increase (7.6x ROI on $50M investment)
Formalized business sector enabling better policy
forBusinesses: Access to formal economy benefits (loans, contracts, legal protection)

keyPoints.title: Component 6: Budget & Timeline
budgetPrinciples: Right-sized for scope (not inflated, not unrealistic)

breakdown: Technical assistance: $15M (advisors, capacity building for government)

keyPoints.title: Component 7: Risk Mitigation

examples.mitigation: Extensive user research, business associations outreach, incentives for early adopters
examples.contingency: Adjust outreach strategy based on pilot data

examples.risk: Tax authority can't process increased registrations
examples.mitigation: Capacity assessment and strengthening as part of project
examples.contingency: Phase rollout to match tax authority capacity

examples.risk: Technology doesn't work in low-connectivity areas

examples.mitigation: Early engagement with business associations and political stakeholders
examples.contingency: Focus on voluntary registration, not enforcement

keyPoints.whyItMatters: Shows you've thought through what can go wrong and aren't naively optimistic. Builds funder confidence.

components.revenueModel: Small registration fee (reduced from current $50 to $10) covers platform operating costs - Self-sustaining after Year 3
capacityBuilding: Government staff trained to operate and maintain platform
Local technology firms capable of supporting system
Knowledge transfer to government IT department
institutionalEmbedding: Platform integrated into official tax authority systems
Champions within government to sustain momentum
components.whyItMatters: Funders don't want to fund forever. Show this will last beyond their support.

content.keyInsight: A strong offer design has clear problem, logical approach, measurable outcomes, realistic budget/timeline, identified risks with mitigation, and sustainability plan. It's both ambitious (worth doing) and achievable (can actually be done).

exercises.prompt: Take a DPI need you're familiar with. Design a complete offer including all 8 components: problem statement, theory of change, approach, outcomes, value proposition, budget, risks, and sustainability. Test it: Is it clear? Logical? Evidence-based? Feasible? Ambitious? Realistic? Aligned?
Review a real proposal you've seen. Evaluate it against the 8 components framework. What's strong? What's missing? What red flags do you see? How would you strengthen it?

modules.title: Proposal Development - Turning Concept into Compelling Document

content.overview: A strong offer design needs to become a compelling proposal document that funders actually read and approve. This requires structuring proposals effectively, writing compellingly, adapting to different funder formats, and incorporating feedback efficiently.

elements: Problem in one compelling paragraph with data
sections.rule: Most decision-makers only read executive summary. Make it count.

elements: Current approaches and why they're insufficient

principles.good: In 2024, 47% of rural health facilities lacked basic medical supplies for more than 15 days per month, forcing 280,000 patients to travel to urban centers for routine care

principles.guidance: Too little data: Looks like guesswork. Too much data: Overwhelms reader. Right amount: Key stats that prove problem scale and solution impact

principles.example: Amina, a 32-year-old mother of three in Kibera, Nairobi, needs government services - birth certificates for her children, health records, social assistance. But without formal identity documentation, she's invisible to the system. She represents 5.2 million Kenyans who lack official identity.

principles.guidance: Don't assume funder sees the connection. Spell out: IF we do X, THEN Y happens BECAUSE of Z. Provide evidence for each causal link.

emphasis: Heavy emphasis on economic analysis (cost-benefit, IRR)
Theory of change upfront and central
Less emphasis on fiduciary (they trust you or they don't)

keyPoints.title: Incorporating Feedback

commonPatterns.feedback: Not clear how this is innovative
commonPatterns.response: Add section comparing to existing approaches, highlighting novel elements
commonPatterns.dont: Claim everything is innovative when it's not

commonPatterns.response: Provide more detailed justification, show benchmarks
commonPatterns.consider: Phasing or reducing scope if genuinely too high

commonPatterns.response: Strengthen causal logic, add evidence for assumptions
commonPatterns.test: Can you defend each IF-THEN with data or research?

commonPatterns.response: Add detailed transition plan, revenue model, capacity building
commonPatterns.beHonest: If it genuinely requires ongoing funding, say so

integrationProcess: Categorize feedback (substantive vs formatting, required vs suggested)
For substantive feedback, strengthen core offer if valid
For feedback that conflicts with implementer needs, discuss trade-offs honestly
Track changes and explain what you revised

content.keyInsight: Great proposals balance comprehensiveness with readability, data with narrative, ambition with realism. They make funder's job easy: 'This is fundable.'

exercises.prompt: Take your offer design from Module 4. Write a compelling 2-page executive summary that would make a funder want to read more. Include: problem (1 paragraph with data), solution (1 paragraph), team credibility, request, and expected impact.
Take the same offer. Write three different 1-paragraph framings for World Bank, Gates Foundation, and USAID. Same underlying offer, different emphasis for each funder's priorities.

modules.title: Multi-Party Alignment - Getting Everyone on Board

content.overview: Real DPI offers involve complex stakeholder ecosystems with competing interests - multiple implementers, funders, government agencies, technical partners. Success requires navigating power dynamics, building consensus, addressing hidden agendas, and creating durable agreements.

keyPoints.title: Mapping the Full Stakeholder Ecosystem
realEcosystem: Primary Implementer (e.g., Government Ministry) - official lead
Technical Implementer (e.g., Bhashini) - does the work
Funder(s) - often multiple with different priorities
Government oversight (Finance, Planning, Audit) - approval authority
Beneficiaries (citizens, businesses) - actually use the solution
keyPoints.insight: Each has different interests, different power, different constraints

keyPoints.title: Power Dynamics and Politics
informalPower: Minister's Chief of Staff might have real decision authority
Funder's country director influenced by HQ priorities
Permanent Secretary might resist if not bought in
keyPoints.warning: Don't assume formal org chart = real power

managingAsymmetricPower.scenario: World Bank ($50M) + small local NGO ($500K TA)
managingAsymmetricPower.mitigation: Explicitly value NGO's local knowledge, give them defined role in governance. NGO leads community engagement, World Bank leads infrastructure

managingAsymmetricPower.risk: Ministry imposes requirements that don't match implementer capacity
managingAsymmetricPower.mitigation: Honest conversation about capacity constraints, phased approach

keyPoints.title: Building Consensus Through Consultative Process

activities: Understand each stakeholder's interests privately
Identify concerns they won't voice in group
Test initial concept and get input
Build relationships before formal meetings
Align implementers before bringing in funders
Align funders before joint meeting
Address conflicts in smaller settings first
Present concept incorporating input from Stages 1-2
Facilitate discussion with clear process
Document agreements and action items
Identify remaining issues for offline resolution
Revise offer based on stakeholder input
Circulate revised concept for feedback
Address objections individually
Build toward final consensus

keyPoints.dont: Present fully-formed offer to large group and expect approval
keyPoints.do: Build consensus through iterative, layered process

patterns.howToSurface: What concerns do you have that we should address?
patterns.howToAddress: Find ways they benefit or aren't threatened

patterns.hidden: We don't have capacity and are embarrassed to admit it
patterns.howToSurface: What support would you need to successfully implement?

patterns.stated: We need more time to consider...
patterns.hidden: We're not bought in but don't want to say no publicly
patterns.howToSurface: Ask directly in 1-on-1: What would make you comfortable?
patterns.howToAddress: Address real concern or accept they're not on board

keyPoints.title: Creating Durable Agreements
keyPoints.challenge: People agree in meeting, then don't follow through

elements: Steering Committee (strategic oversight) - who's on it?
Assume key champions will leave (they always do)
Broaden the coalition (not dependent on one person)

content.keyInsight: Multi-party alignment requires patient, iterative relationship-building. You're not just aligning on technical proposal - you're building trust and shared commitment among parties with different interests, power, and constraints.

exercises.prompt: Map the full stakeholder ecosystem for a complex DPI offer (e.g., digital ID with government, tech provider, 3 funders, multiple ministries). Identify: formal power, informal power, interests, concerns. What's your alignment strategy?

Role-play a stakeholder workshop where you're trying to build consensus among parties with different priorities. Practice: How do you surface concerns? How do you find common ground? How do you handle one party dominating?

content.overview: All DPI offers face risks - technical, capacity, political, financial, adoption. Your job is to identify likely risks, reduce their probability, plan smart responses, and address funder and implementer objections constructively.

risks: Training doesn't stick (people trained but don't apply)
Government can't provide co-funding as promised
Users don't adopt solution (despite building it)
Informal systems more attractive than formal

keyPoints.title: Risk Mitigation Framework
keyPoints.framework: For each risk: (1) Likelihood (high/medium/low), (2) Impact (high/medium/low), (3) Mitigation (what reduces likelihood), (4) Contingency (what if it happens anyway)

examples.mitigation: Extensive capacity building, embedded advisors, phased approach, mentoring
examples.contingency: If capacity insufficient, extend timeline or reduce scope

examples.impact: High (successful technology with no users = failure)
examples.mitigation: User-centered design, extensive testing, incentives, easy opt-in
examples.contingency: If adoption low after 6 months, rapid iteration based on user feedback

keyPoints.prioritization: Focus most attention on high-likelihood, high-impact risks

approach: Acknowledge: 'You're right that this is ambitious...'
Provide evidence: 'Here's why we think it's achievable: [similar examples, pilot data, capacity assessment]'
Offer adjustment: 'We could phase this - prove Phase 1, then scale in Phase 2'

objections.objection: We're not confident in implementer capacity
approach: Acknowledge: 'Capacity is a legitimate concern. Here's how we're addressing it...'
Offer evidence: 'Implementer has delivered [X, Y, Z]. For new areas, we're building capacity through [specific plan]'
Consider: Bringing in additional technical partners to supplement capacity
Ask: 'What budget range did you have in mind?'
Justify: 'Here's how we arrived at this budget [breakdown, benchmarks]'
Offer options: 'We could reduce scope to [X] for $[Y], or phase over longer period'
Don't: Agree to cut budget without cutting scope (recipe for failure)

objections.objection: We've tried this before and it failed
approach: Learn: 'Tell me about that experience. What went wrong?'
Acknowledge: 'That's valuable learning. Here's how our approach differs: [specific]'
Build confidence: 'We're specifically designing to avoid those failure modes'

keyPoints.title: Building Contingency Plans
structure: Trigger: What indicates the risk is materializing?
Decision authority: Who decides to activate contingency?
Resources: What's needed to execute contingency?

example.trigger: Platform response time >5 seconds at scale, or >2% error rate
response: Week 1: Diagnose root cause, implement quick fixes
Week 2-4: If not resolved, bring in external technical experts
Month 2: If still not resolved, consider alternative technology platform
example.authority: Technical Committee with Steering Committee approval for platform change
example.resources: $500K contingency budget for additional technical support

content.keyInsight: Risk management is not about eliminating risk (impossible). It's about identifying likely risks, reducing their probability, and having smart responses when they materialize anyway.

exercises.prompt: Take a DPI offer you're working on. Identify the top 5 risks. For each: assess likelihood and impact, design mitigation strategy, plan contingency response. Which risks deserve most attention?
Role-play: Partner gives you common funder objections. Practice responding constructively: listen, acknowledge, provide evidence, offer adjustments. Don't get defensive or dismiss concerns.

modules.title: From Approval to Implementation - Ensuring Funded Proposals Actually Deliver

content.overview: Getting funding approved is just the beginning. Implementation is where proposals meet reality. Success requires navigating the transition from concept to operations, adaptive management, genuine learning, stakeholder engagement, and sustained momentum through multi-year journeys.

keyPoints.title: The Valley of Death: Approval to Launch
commonPattern: Months of work to get approval
whyThisHappens: Proposal was concept, implementation is real work
Team that wrote proposal ≠ team that implements
Assumptions in proposal don't match reality
Stakeholder attention shifts to other priorities

activities: Assemble implementation team (may be different from proposal team)
Review proposal with implementers: 'Here's what we committed, here's how we do it'
Validate assumptions: Do rapid assessment of key assumptions in proposal
Develop Year 1 detailed workplan
Set up governance structures
Begin stakeholder engagement
Start with pilot or proof-of-concept (don't go straight to full scale)
Test assumptions: Does technical approach work? Do users adopt? Is capacity sufficient?
Adjust based on learning: Proposal was best guess, reality is evidence
Get early wins: Build confidence with quick, visible progress

keyPoints.dont: Treat proposal as contract that cannot change
keyPoints.do: Treat proposal as hypothesis to be validated and refined

keyPoints.title: Setting Up Governance

structures.members: Funder representatives, government leadership, key stakeholders
structures.decisions: Scope changes, budget reallocations, strategy shifts

structures.members: Implementation team leads, technical experts, government counterparts
structures.decisions: Workplan adjustments, technical approach, resource allocation

structures.structure: Program Director, technical leads, M&E specialist, operations
structures.accountabilities: Deliver on workplan, manage budget, report progress

whatWorks: Action-oriented (meetings lead to decisions and actions)

keyPoints.title: Meaningful M&E (Not Reporting Theater)

questions: Are we delivering what we promised?
Are we on track with timeline and budget?
What have we accomplished?
Is our theory of change working?
What's working and what isn't?
What should we adjust?
Are we on track to hit milestones?
Where are bottlenecks?
Where do we need to focus resources?

outcomeIndicators: Number of citizens registered in digital ID system
Average time to complete government service transaction

keyPoints.dont: Collect data just to satisfy funder reporting
keyPoints.do: Collect data that helps you manage and improve the program

keyPoints.title: Managing When Reality Differs from Proposal
keyPoints.thisWillHappen: Proposals are estimates and assumptions. Reality always differs.

scenarios.diagnose: Capacity gaps? Technical complexity? Political delays?
options: Extend timeline (if funder agrees and budget allows)
Reduce scope (deliver less but deliver well)

scenarios.example: We built digital service, but citizens aren't using it
scenarios.diagnose: Why not adopting? Awareness? Access? Trust? Usability?
scenarios.adapt: Rapid iteration based on user feedback
scenarios.communicate: 'We learned X, therefore we're adjusting approach to Y'

options: Reframe program to align with new priorities (if genuine alignment)
In extreme cases: Wind down gracefully

keyPoints.title: Maintaining Momentum
keyPoints.challenge: Year 1: excitement and energy. Years 2-3: the slog - Initial excitement fades, hard work of scaling begins, stakeholder attention shifts

actions: Keep funders engaged (not just annual reports)
Broader coalition than initial core team
Broaden leadership (not dependent on one person)

keyPoints.title: Closing Well

months6to12BeforeEnd: Sustainability assessment: What will continue? What needs ongoing funding?
Transition planning: Who takes over what?
Knowledge documentation: Lessons learned, good practices, tools/templates
Impact evaluation: Did we achieve what we set out to? What evidence?
closingActivities: Transition activities: Hand over to government, local partners, or next phase funder
Close out reporting: Comprehensive final report on outcomes and learning
Dissemination: Share lessons with broader DPI community

exitWell: Leave implementer stronger than you found them
Leave tools and knowledge that outlast the program
Leave relationships that enable future collaboration
Leave evidence that can inform next generation of work

content.keyInsight: Getting funding approved is just the beginning. Implementation is where proposals meet reality. Success requires adaptive management, genuine learning, stakeholder engagement, and sustained momentum through multi-year journeys.

exercises.prompt: Your DPI proposal just got approved. Design your inception phase (first 90 days). What are your priorities? How will you validate key assumptions? What's your detailed Year 1 workplan? How will you set up governance?

You're 18 months into implementation. User adoption is 30% of target. Your theory of change assumed 'if we build it, they will come' but that's not happening. What do you do? How do you diagnose the problem? What adaptations would you consider? How do you communicate with funder?

assessmentApproach: Case-based evaluation with coaching feedback. Learners demonstrate offer crafting through: (1) Need identification exercises with real scenarios, (2) Funder mapping and framing exercises, (3) Full proposal development for realistic DPI scenario, (4) Peer review and iteration, (5) Presentation to mock funder panel
targetAudience: DPI advisors who connect governments with funding, government officials responsible for resource mobilization, technical advisors who translate needs into proposals, program managers who work across implementer-funder boundaries
